## Data

For this homework, we are going to being using the `survey` data set. These data contains the responses of 237 Statistics I students at the University of Adelaide to a number of questions. You can find the variable names and descriptions by clicking the link [here](https://rdrr.io/cran/MASS/man/survey.html). We are going to use a cleaned up data set that **only looks at students younger than 25 years old**. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
survey <- na.omit(survey) |>
  filter(Age < 25)
```

## Exercise 3 (15 points)

We are now going to fit a multiple linear regression model, and include the categorical variable `Smoke`. Smoke has four levels: Heavy, Never, Occas, and Regul. The plot for your model can be seen below.  

```{r}
#| echo: false

# 1. Prepare the data (as in your prompt)
survey_data <- na.omit(survey) |>
  filter(Age < 25)

# 2. Fit the Additive Model (Shared Slope)
# The formula Pulse ~ Age + Smoke is the additive model
model_additive <- lm(Pulse ~ Age + Smoke, data = survey_data)

# 3. Generate Predictions and Add to Data Frame
# Create a data frame of predictions for the fitted model
survey_data$Pulse_Fitted <- predict(model_additive, newdata = survey_data)

# 4. Create the ggplot
ggplot(survey_data, aes(x = Age, y = Pulse, color = Smoke)) +
  # Original Data Points
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  # Fitted Regression Lines (The shared slope is key here)
  # The geom_line will draw parallel lines because the model is additive.
  geom_line(aes(y = Pulse_Fitted), linewidth = 1) +
  # Customization
  labs(
    title = "Additive Linear Model of Pulse vs Age, Grouped by Smoking Habit",
    subtitle = "Same Slope for Age Across All Smoking Categories",
    y = "Pulse Rate",
    x = "Age (Years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")
```

a) Explain in 1-2 sentences why this is an additive model, and not an interaction model. 

b) Please see your model output for your additive model below. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
model2 <- lm(Pulse ~ Age + Smoke, data = survey)
tidy(model2)
```

Write out the simplified model for someone who smokes **Heavy**. 

c) Write out the simplified model for someone who smokes **Never**. 

d) Interpret -0.828 in the context of the problem. 


## Exercise 4 (15 points)

We are now going to fit an interaction model, and include the categorical variable `Smoke`. Smoke has four levels: Heavy, Never, Occas, and Regul. The plot for your model can be seen below.  

```{r}
#| echo: false
# 1. Prepare the data (as per the original prompt)
survey_data <- na.omit(survey) |>
  filter(Age < 25)

# 2. Fit the Interaction Model (Different Slopes)
# The formula Pulse ~ Age * Smoke is the interaction model
model_interaction <- lm(Pulse ~ Age * Smoke, data = survey_data)

# 3. Generate Predictions and Add to Data Frame
# Create a data frame of predictions for the fitted model
survey_data$Pulse_Fitted_Interaction <- predict(model_interaction, newdata = survey_data)

# 4. Create the ggplot
ggplot(survey_data, aes(x = Age, y = Pulse, color = Smoke)) +
  # Original Data Points
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  # Fitted Regression Lines (The different slopes are key here)
  # The geom_line will draw non-parallel lines because of the interaction term.
  geom_line(aes(y = Pulse_Fitted_Interaction), linewidth = 1) +
  # Customization
  labs(
    title = "Interaction Model of Pulse vs Age, Grouped by Smoking Habit",
    subtitle = "Different Slopes for Age Across All Smoking Categories",
    y = "Pulse Rate",
    x = "Age (Years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")
```

a) In 1-2 sentences, explain why this is an interaction model instead of a additive model. 

b) Please see your model output for your interaction model below. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
model3 <- lm(Pulse ~ Age * Smoke, data = survey)
tidy(model3)
```

c) Write out the simplified model for someone who smokes **Heavy**. 

d) Write out the simplified model for someone who smokes **Never**. 

## Exercise 5 (15 points)

We are now going to **test** if it makes sense to include the interaction term between Smoke and Age, versus our additive model. 

a) Write out the null and alternative hypothesis in proper notation below: 

$H_o:$ 

$H_a:$ 

b) In 1-2 sentences, describe why our reduced model (additive) is entirely nested into the interaction model (full).


c) List out the other assumptions you need to check for this hypothesis test. I'm not asking you to check them, I'm asking you to name them. 


d) Please see the follow `Anova` table from R below.

```{r}
#| echo: false
# 1. Fit the Reduced Model (MR: Flipper Length ~ Bill Length)
model_reduced <- lm(Pulse ~ Age + Smoke, data = survey)

# 2. Fit the Full Model (MF: Flipper Length ~ Bill Length + Species)
model_full <- lm(Pulse ~ Age * Smoke, data = survey)

# 3. Perform the Model Comparison F-test
anova(model_reduced, model_full)
```

Report your F-statistic. That is identify and write what your F-statistic is from the output. 

e) That F-statistic is created using the following formula:

$$F = \frac{\frac{RSS_R - RSS_F}{df_R - df_F}}{\frac{RSS_F}{df_F}}$$


The residual sums of squares is calculated as so: 

$$\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$$


The R represents your reduced model. The F represents your full model. 


$\text{RSS}_R = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = 20154.72$

$\text{RSS}_F = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = 19998.49$


Use this information, and output from part d, to show exactly the F-statistic was calculated that you identified in part d.
